subject: Islamic Studies
q: The Takbirat recited after the obligatory prayers during the days of Eid-ul-Adha and Hajj are called:
explanation: Takbirat-e-Tashriq (“Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar, La ilaha illallah…”) are said after the obligatory prayers from the Day of Arafah through the Days of Tashriq.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The sacrifice (Qurbani) on Eid-ul-Adha commemorates the example of:
explanation: It recalls Ibrahim’s (AS) readiness to sacrifice his son at Allah’s command and the ram sent as ransom.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The sacrifice of an animal on the birth of a child, as a Sunnah, is called:
explanation: Aqiqah is offered in thanks for a newborn, customarily on the seventh day, when the child is also named.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The special form of congregational prayer offered in a state of war or danger is called:
explanation: Surah An-Nisa describes how the army divides so that one group prays while the other stands guard.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Which day of the week is called ‘Sayyid-ul-Ayyam’ (the chief of days) in Hadith?
explanation: Hadith describe Friday as the best and chief of days, on which Adam (AS) was created and the Hour will be established.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Which of the following is a Qur’anic name of the Ka‘bah?
explanation: Surah Al-Hajj calls the Ka‘bah “Al-Bait-ul-Atiq”, the Ancient House.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The semicircular enclosed area adjoining the Ka‘bah, regarded as part of it, is called:
explanation: Hatim (Hijr Isma‘il) was left outside when the Quraysh rebuilt the Ka‘bah with limited funds; Tawaf must be made outside it.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: A Hajj performed on behalf of another person who is unable or deceased is called:
explanation: Hadith permit performing Hajj on behalf of someone who cannot do it because of death or permanent incapacity.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: An animal sacrifice required as a penalty for violating certain rules of Ihram or Hajj is called:
explanation: Dam is an expiatory sacrifice for lapses such as omitting a wajib rite or committing a prohibited act while in Ihram.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Seeking forgiveness from Allah by saying ‘Astaghfirullah’ is called:
explanation: Istighfar is asking forgiveness; Istikharah is seeking guidance, Isti‘adhah seeking refuge and Istisqa praying for rain.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: A person who has entered the state of Ihram is called:
explanation: A Muhrim must observe the restrictions of Ihram; a Mu‘takif is one in I‘tikaf.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The niche in the wall of a mosque indicating the direction of the Qiblah is called:
explanation: The Imam stands in or before the Mihrab; the Minbar is the pulpit from which the Khutbah is delivered.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Which obligatory prayer consists of three rak‘ahs?
explanation: Maghrib has three obligatory rak‘ahs, Fajr two, and Zuhr, Asr and Isha four each for a resident.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The four primary sources of Islamic law, in order of priority, are:
explanation: Jurists turn first to the Qur’an, then the Sunnah, then the consensus of scholars, and then analogical reasoning.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: After the Qur’an, the second primary source of Islamic law is:
explanation: The Sunnah explains and supplements the Qur’an; the Qur’an itself commands obedience to the Messenger.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: What is the literal meaning of ‘Ijma’?
explanation: Ijma literally means agreement or consensus; in Islamic law it is the consensus of qualified jurists on a ruling.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: In Islamic jurisprudence, Ijma is the:
o: Agreement of qualified jurists of the Ummah on a legal ruling after the Prophet (PBUH)
Opinion of a single eminent scholar
Decision of the ruler of the time
Custom of the people of a region
explanation: Ijma requires the agreement of the Mujtahids of a period; it derives its authority from the Qur’an and Sunnah.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: ‘Qiyas’ in Islamic law means:
explanation: Qiyas extends the ruling of a case found in the texts to a new case that shares the same effective cause.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: In Qiyas, the common effective cause linking the original case and the new case is called:
explanation: Qiyas has four elements: Asl (original case), Far‘ (new case), Hukm (ruling) and ‘Illah (effective cause).

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Extending the prohibition of wine to other intoxicating drugs because they share the effect of intoxication is an example of:
explanation: Wine is prohibited in the Qur’an because it intoxicates; by analogy the same ruling applies to every intoxicant.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Ijtihad refers to:
o: Independent legal reasoning by a qualified jurist
explanation: Ijtihad, from juhd (effort), is a qualified scholar’s utmost effort to derive a ruling from the sources.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: A scholar qualified to exercise Ijtihad is called:
explanation: A Mujtahid has the knowledge of the Qur’an, Sunnah, Arabic and legal methodology needed to derive rulings; a Muqallid follows one.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The conversation of the Holy Prophet (PBUH) with which Companion, on sending him to Yemen, is cited as the basis of Ijtihad?
explanation: Mu‘adh (RA) said he would judge by the Book, then the Sunnah, and then exercise his own reasoning, and the Prophet (PBUH) approved.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Following the opinion of a recognised Imam or school without examining the evidence oneself is called:
explanation: Taqlid is the practice of a non-specialist relying on a qualified jurist; Talfiq is mixing opinions of different schools.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The principle of Istihsan (juristic preference) is particularly associated with the school of:
explanation: Hanafi jurists used Istihsan to depart from a strict analogy for a stronger reason; Imam Shafi‘i famously criticised it.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: ‘Maslahah Mursalah’, a principle especially associated with the Maliki school, means:
o: Consideration of public interest not specifically addressed by the texts
explanation: Maslahah Mursalah permits rulings that serve a genuine public benefit where no text affirms or rejects it, such as the Companions’ compilation of the Qur’an.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: In Islamic law, recognised custom that does not conflict with the texts is called:
explanation: Jurists take sound custom into account in matters such as contracts and maintenance, provided it does not contradict Shariah.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The principle that a state of affairs is presumed to continue until evidence shows it has changed is called:
explanation: By Istishab, for example, a person in Wudu remains so until certain that it has been broken.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Prohibiting a lawful act because it is likely to lead to something forbidden is based on the principle of:
explanation: Sadd adh-Dhara’i means blocking the means: where a permissible act generally leads to harm, the path to harm is closed.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Which of the following is NOT one of the five classical objectives (Maqasid) of Shariah?
explanation: The classical Maqasid are the protection of religion, life, intellect, lineage and property.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The theory of Maqasid al-Shariah was systematically developed by Imam al-Shatibi in his book:
explanation: Abu Ishaq al-Shatibi of Granada set out the higher objectives of Islamic law in Al-Muwafaqat.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The prohibition of intoxicants primarily serves which objective of Shariah?
explanation: Intoxicants cloud the mind; their prohibition protects ‘aql (intellect), one of the five essential objectives.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The discipline that studies the principles and methodology of deriving legal rulings is called:
explanation: Fiqh is the body of rulings, while Usul-ul-Fiqh studies the sources and methods by which those rulings are derived.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Imam Shafi‘i’s book, regarded as the first systematic work on Usul-ul-Fiqh, is:
explanation: In Al-Risalah Imam Shafi‘i set out the authority of the Sunnah, Ijma and Qiyas, laying the foundation of legal theory.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The literal meaning of ‘Fiqh’ is:
explanation: Fiqh means deep understanding; technically it is knowledge of practical Shariah rulings derived from detailed evidence.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The word ‘Shariah’ literally means:
o: A path leading to a watering place
explanation: As water is the source of life, Shariah is the clear path to spiritual life laid down by Allah.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: An act that is neither rewarded nor punished and is left to one’s choice is called:
explanation: Mubah (permissible) acts, such as ordinary eating and walking, carry no reward or sin in themselves.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: An act whose avoidance is rewarded but whose commission is not punished is:
explanation: Makruh means disliked; the Shariah discourages it without making it forbidden.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: An act that is rewarded if done but not punished if left is called:
explanation: Mandub acts are recommended, like voluntary prayers and charity; omitting them is not sinful.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: An obligation which, if performed by some members of the community, relieves the rest is called:
explanation: Funeral prayer and acquiring essential professions are collective duties; if no one performs them, the whole community is sinful.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: In Hanafi usage, an obligation established by evidence that is less than decisive is termed:
explanation: Hanafis distinguish Fard, proved by decisive evidence, from Wajib, proved by probable evidence, such as the Witr prayer.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: A concession allowed in special circumstances, such as shortening prayer on a journey, is called:
explanation: ‘Azimah is the original rule, while Rukhsah is a relaxation granted because of hardship.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: A person who is legally responsible for religious obligations is called:
explanation: A Mukallaf is an adult of sound mind upon whom the duties of Shariah are binding.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi‘i and Hanbali are:
explanation: These four Sunni madhahib are schools of jurisprudence named after their founding Imams.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The Maliki school of Fiqh originated in:
explanation: Imam Malik lived and taught in Madinah and gave weight to the practice of its people (‘Amal Ahl al-Madinah).

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The Hanafi school of Fiqh developed in:
explanation: Imam Abu Hanifa taught in Kufa in Iraq, where his students Abu Yusuf and Muhammad al-Shaybani developed the school.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: ‘Kitab al-Umm’, a major work of Fiqh, was written by:
explanation: Kitab al-Umm contains Imam Shafi‘i’s legal doctrines, compiled in Egypt where he spent his final years.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Most Sunni Muslims in Pakistan follow which school of Fiqh?
explanation: The Hanafi school spread with Turkic and Mughal rule across Central and South Asia and is dominant in Pakistan.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The Maliki school is predominant in:
explanation: Maliki Fiqh spread through Andalusia and the Maghrib and remains dominant in North and West Africa.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The Ja‘fari school of jurisprudence is named after:
explanation: The Ja‘fari school, followed by Shia Muslims, is named after Imam Ja‘far al-Sadiq, a renowned scholar of Madinah.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The Majallah al-Ahkam al-Adliyyah, a codified civil law based on Hanafi Fiqh, was issued by the:
explanation: The Ottomans promulgated the Majallah in the 1870s, one of the first codifications of Islamic civil law.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Fatawa-e-Alamgiri, a compilation of Hanafi law, was prepared under the patronage of:
explanation: Aurangzeb commissioned a board of scholars to compile Fatawa-e-Alamgiri (Al-Fatawa al-Hindiyyah) as a reference for courts.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Al-Hidayah, a standard text of Hanafi Fiqh, was written by:
explanation: Al-Marghinani’s Al-Hidayah became a core Hanafi text and was translated into English for courts in British India.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The waiting period a woman observes after divorce or the death of her husband is called:
explanation: During Iddat a woman may not remarry; it ensures clarity of lineage and allows reconciliation after revocable divorce.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Dissolution of marriage at the instance of the wife, usually by returning the Mahr, is called:
explanation: Khula lets a wife obtain release from marriage, as in the case of the wife of Thabit bin Qais (RA) who returned her garden.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: When a husband likens his wife to his mother or another prohibited relative in order to deny her marital rights, the act is called:
explanation: Zihar was a pre-Islamic practice; the Qur’an condemned it and required expiation before the husband may resume marital relations.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: A husband’s oath to abstain from marital relations with his wife is called:
explanation: The Qur’an allows a husband who takes such an oath four months to return, after which the marriage cannot be left in suspense.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Li‘an refers to:
o: Mutual oaths of husband and wife when he accuses her of adultery without witnesses
explanation: Surah An-Nur prescribes Li‘an: each spouse swears and invokes Allah’s curse or wrath if lying, after which they are separated.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The right of custody and upbringing of a young child is called:
explanation: Hadanah is physical care of the child, usually given to the mother in early years; Wilayah is guardianship over the child’s person and property.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The obligation of a husband to provide food, clothing and shelter for his wife is called:
explanation: Nafaqah (maintenance) is the husband’s duty regardless of the wife’s own wealth.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: Kinship established through breastfeeding is called:
explanation: The Qur’an lists foster mothers and sisters among those one may not marry; Musaharat is kinship by marriage.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: A relative with whom marriage is permanently prohibited is called:
explanation: Surah An-Nisa lists the Mahram relatives, such as mother, sister, daughter, aunt and niece.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: A divorce after which the husband may take his wife back during the Iddat without a new Nikah is called:
explanation: In a revocable divorce the marriage can be resumed during Iddat; after it ends, a fresh Nikah is required.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: In a Nikah contract, ‘Ijab’ and ‘Qabul’ mean:
explanation: A valid Nikah requires an offer by one party and acceptance by the other in the same sitting before witnesses.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: In Islamic law, Nikah is essentially:
o: A sacrament that can never be dissolved
A purely private promise without legal effect
A contract between the parties with mutual rights and duties
explanation: Nikah is a civil contract (‘aqd) based on consent, offer, acceptance and Mahr; it can be dissolved through Talaq or Khula.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The wealth or property left by a deceased person is called:
explanation: Taraka is the estate from which funeral expenses, debts and bequests are paid before division among heirs.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: The branch of Islamic jurisprudence dealing with the law of inheritance is called:
explanation: Faraid (fixed shares) are prescribed mainly in Surah An-Nisa; Ilm-ul-Aruz is prosody.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: A Muslim may bequeath to non-heirs, without the heirs’ consent, up to:
explanation: The Prophet (PBUH) told Sa‘d bin Abi Waqqas (RA) that one-third is the limit, “and a third is much”.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: According to Islamic law, the debts of a deceased person are paid:
o: After the heirs receive their shares
Before the bequests are executed and shares distributed
explanation: Surah An-Nisa repeatedly states that shares are given “after any bequest he made or debt”; debts take priority over heirs.

subject: Islamic Studies
q: A wife’s share in her deceased husband’s estate when he leaves children is:
explanation: Surah An-Nisa fixes the wife’s share at one-quarter if there are no children and one-eighth if there are.
